writing.exampleCaption: Classification checklist for Grid Flood Fill
writing.explanation:
A problem is a good match for Grid Flood Fill when it asks for islands, image fill, maze regions. Here the concrete task is: Return the size of the component containing row 1 column 1. The visible input `[[1,0,0],[1,1,0],[0,1,1]]` is an example, not a definition of the whole problem. Ask what operations the solution must support and what the input guarantees. Choose DFS for depth-oriented exploration and BFS for equal-cost layers; directed edges and disconnected components change the plan. The right choice follows from those guarantees, not from a familiar noun in the prompt.

The decisive invariant is: Treat cells as graph nodes and traverse only neighbors satisfying the region predicate. Try to say why it applies to the task without quoting the implementation. Which fact becomes known after one update, and which possible answers remain? Traversal marks reached vertices so each reachable part is processed deliberately. Define when a vertex becomes seen: on insertion or removal. If that claim cannot be maintained on a legal input, the pattern is wrong or one of its preconditions is missing. A counterexample is more useful than a vague warning: change one property of the sample, trace the first two steps, and identify the exact claim that fails.

Compare costs before committing. The advertised bound is O(rows*cols) time · O(rows*cols) space worst; identify the operation responsible for it and the extra memory it needs. Then compare a straightforward alternative: a direct scan, full sort, or repeated recomputation may be easier but can pay for the same work many times. Do not choose the more elaborate method just because it has a famous name. For the sample, predict `5` and explain which part of the state lets the method reach that result.

When the prompt is ambiguous, ask about input size, ordering, duplicates, and required output format. Test an isolated vertex, a cycle, duplicate edges, and a graph whose starting vertex reaches only one component. An adjacency list and VecDeque make breadth-first work explicit. Mark before enqueuing to avoid duplicate frontier entries. The Rust sketch can show a useful primitive without proving that the whole task is solved; connect each primitive to the requested output. You should be able to name a fitting case, a near miss, and the assumption separating them before writing the first line.
